speaker: Raquel Urtasun
title: An AI-First Approach to Enable Self Driving at Scale, with Raquel Urtasun of Waabi
question: In autonomous driving, why does simulating abstract bounding-box trajectories to test the motion planner fail to verify system safety?
guest: If you look at the industry and you look at where simulation is used at scale today, it's only really used in order to test the motion planner. In particular, scenarios are generated where the input is simple abstract representations of the scene, for example, bounding boxes representing actors as well as their trajectories, and then basically only one model is tested. Now, the problem of this is twofold. First is that you don't test the entire software stack, so you can't really verify the safety of your system if you're only testing a single component. Furthermore, the input for this test, which tries to mimic what is the output of the perception and prediction system, doesn't have the same level of noise characteristics as the real system has. So even that subsystem that you're trying to verify, you don't really verify it fully.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Simulating abstract bounding-box trajectories tests the planner in isolation, under the assumption that perception is perfect. The planner receives clean, ground-truth object boxes and tracks, but in the real vehicle it consumes the output of a perception and prediction stack working from raw camera, lidar and radar data. That output contains missed detections, false positives, localization and velocity errors, latency, flicker, and misclassifications, and these errors are correlated with the scene itself (occlusion, lighting, weather, unusual objects, distance).

Because the abstract simulation skips sensor data entirely, it cannot reveal how perception errors propagate downstream and change the planner's behavior. A planner that drives flawlessly on perfect boxes may brake late or collide when a pedestrian is detected half a second late. Conversely, perception metrics alone do not tell you which errors matter for driving.

Safety is a property of the whole closed-loop system, including the interactions between modules, so verifying it requires either end-to-end testing with realistic sensor simulation (photorealistic or neural rendering) or injecting realistic, statistically validated perception error models into the abstract simulation. Even then, the simulation-to-reality gap must itself be validated.

points.why: Testing the planner in isolation leaves the other modules and their interactions unverified.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Simulating abstract bounding-box trajectories isolates the motion planner from the rest of the autonomous stack, testing planning logic on idealized inputs rather than verifying whole-system safety. Bypassing sensor simulation, perception, and prediction hides realistic upstream failures such as missed detections, false positives, tracking jitter, and latency caused by weather, lighting, or occlusion, whose error distributions depend on scene appearance rather than simple synthetic noise. It also breaks closed-loop feedback: in reality, the ego vehicle’s motion continuously changes sensor viewpoints and visibility while provoking reactive behaviors from surrounding road users that replayed or simplified box agents fail to capture. Furthermore, rigid boxes omit safety-critical visual and geometric cues like turn signals, pedestrian posture, articulated trailers, and overhanging cargo. Abstract trajectory checks also frequently neglect low-level vehicle dynamics, actuator delays, and road-friction limits that determine whether a planned path is physically trackable. Because real-world crashes typically stem from compounding, cross-module interactions rather than isolated planning bugs on clean state estimates, bounding-box simulation cannot establish end-to-end system safety.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Testing the planner with abstract bounding-box trajectories assumes perfect perception. The planner is handed clean, complete, correctly labeled object tracks, so the simulation skips the part of the stack where many real failures start. A real vehicle plans from what its sensors and perception system actually produce. That output includes missed detections, false positives, misclassifications, jittery or delayed tracks, wrong size and heading estimates, occlusions, and errors from weather or lighting. Safety is a property of the whole closed loop, not of the planner alone. A planner can look flawless on ground-truth boxes and still brake hard for a phantom object, or fail to yield to a pedestrian who was detected late. Small perception errors also add up over time, and they interact with planning decisions in ways that testing each component separately cannot reveal. Replayed trajectories have a further problem: the other road users don't react realistically to what the ego vehicle does, and scenario coverage is limited. So this kind of testing can check planning logic, but it cannot show that the deployed system is safe. That takes sensor-level or closed-loop simulation plus real-world validation.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Simulating abstract bounding-box trajectories isolates the motion planner from the rest of the autonomous driving stack, leaving critical system-level failure modes untested. First, feeding idealized or synthetically perturbed boxes bypasses the perception pipeline, hiding real-world sensor limitations such as occlusions, glare, adverse weather, latency, false positives, missed detections, and tracking jitter. Because the ego vehicle's own motion continuously alters camera and lidar viewpoints, abstract simulations also miss closed-loop coupling between planning and perception, where a planned maneuver can create new blind spots or degrade object detection. Second, rigid bounding boxes strip away fine-grained geometry and semantic cues—such as overhanging cargo, open doors, road debris, pedestrian posture, or turn signals—that are essential for judging collision risk and intent. Finally, trajectory-level tests often rely on scripted or non-reactive agents and simplified vehicle kinematics, failing to capture realistic multi-agent negotiation, rare long-tail interactions, and low-level control or tire-road dynamics. Consequently, passing bounding-box planner tests demonstrates only narrow algorithmic competence, not end-to-end vehicle safety.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Bounding-box trajectories let you test how a motion planner responds to a specified set of objects and motions. System safety also depends on whether the vehicle detects those objects in time, estimates their positions and velocities accurately, predicts their behavior, and executes the planned maneuver within the vehicle’s physical limits.

Feeding the planner ground-truth boxes can hide failures such as a pedestrian being missed behind a parked car or a vehicle’s speed being misestimated. And if the trajectories are scripted, other road users may follow the same paths regardless of what the ego vehicle does, masking hazards that arise through interaction. A passing test therefore shows that the planner handled the inputs and assumptions of that test. It provides only part of the evidence needed to verify the safety of the full driving system.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer: A bounding-box simulation tests whether the motion planner chooses a safe trajectory given the objects and motions supplied by the simulator. System safety also depends on whether the vehicle detects those objects, estimates their motion in time, and executes the planned maneuver. For example, a planner may brake safely when the simulator supplies a pedestrian’s position, while the real vehicle detects the pedestrian too late to stop. Passing the simulation therefore provides evidence about the planner under the tested assumptions, but it cannot establish that the full driving system is safe.
